title: Bisphenol A and Adiposity in an Inner-City Birth Cohort.
ehr_evidence: Study subjects are participants in the prospective birth cohort of the Columbia Center for Children's Environmental Health (CCCEH) in Northern Manhattan and the South Bronx, New York; BPA concentrations were measured in prenatal and child spot urine samples and anthropometric/bioelectrical impedance outcomes were collected prospectively.
summary: In a prospective inner-city NYC birth cohort of African-American and Dominican mother-child pairs, prenatal and early-childhood urinary BPA exposure was examined in relation to childhood adiposity measures (FMI, %BF, WC, BMIZ) at ages 5 and 7 years.
key_findings: Prenatal urinary BPA was positively associated with age-7 fat mass index (β = 0.31 kg/m2; 95% CI: 0.01, 0.60, p = 0.04), percent body fat (β = 0.79; 95% CI: 0.03, 1.55, p = 0.04), and waist circumference (β = 1.29 cm; 95% CI: 0.29, 2.30, p = 0.01) but not BMIZ or change in BMIZ.

The association of prenatal BPA with FMI was sex-specific, significant among girls (FMI β = 0.48; 95% CI: 0.5, 0.91; WC β = 1.45; 95% CI: 0.5, 2.85) but not boys, with a significant BPA×sex interaction (p = 0.04).
Child (postnatal) urinary BPA concentrations were not associated with FMI, %BF, or WC at age 7 years (all p > 0.05).
Child BPA had a borderline negative association with change in BMIZ from age 5 to 7 years (β = –0.10; 95% CI: –0.02, 0.005, p = 0.06), significant for girls only.
Prenatal BPA was not associated with birth weight.
captured_features: prenatal and child urinary BPA concentrations (specific gravity-adjusted, ln-transformed, tertiles)
population: NYC inner-city birth cohort (Northern Manhattan and South Bronx); African-American and Dominican women aged 18–35 at enrollment in third trimester; children followed to age 7 years
limitations: Single spot urine samples for BPA lead to nondifferential exposure misclassification and likely underestimate true effects.
Lack of dietary data during pregnancy and childhood.
Body composition at age 7 assessed by bioelectrical impedance, not compared to gold-standard reference methods.
No pubertal timing/hormonal data, so pubertal development cannot be excluded as a driver of sex-specific associations.
Missing anthropometric and biomarker data, though IPW suggested loss to follow-up did not bias results.
